name: SIA Project 25 26
description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

To have the option to submit reports without their name being publicly displayed.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Register and Report Urban Issues
branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (llg_001, llg_002, llg_003) focus on establishing and personalizing a citizen's account, which is a prerequisite for participating in the system. The subsequent goals (llg_004, llg_005, llg_006, llg_007) detail the process of submitting comprehensive reports about urban issues. Together, these operations form a complete flow for citizens to engage with a platform designed for reporting community problems.

branch_002.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Their Submitted Reports
branch_002.rationale: The low-level goals collectively aim to provide citizens with comprehensive tools to track the status and history of their submitted reports, receive timely updates, and control their notification preferences. This ensures citizens are well-informed and have agency over their interactions with the reporting system.

branch_003.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire conversation history. This ensures effective and transparent interaction for report resolution.

branch_004.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of allowing citizens to submit reports without their identity being publicly disclosed. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose this option, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it, ensuring the anonymity is maintained.

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Access and Monitor Public Reports
branch_005.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe functionalities that allow citizens to discover (view, filter) and track (subscribe, unsubscribe) publicly available reports submitted by other citizens. These operations are all geared towards providing citizens with the means to stay informed about and engage with community-reported information.

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to Access and View Public Reports
branch_006.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions by a non-registered user to retrieve, display, and filter public reports using various interfaces and methods. They collectively contribute to the overarching goal of making public reports accessible and viewable to non-registered users.

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Access to Reporting Statistics
branch_007.rationale: Both low-level goals describe functionalities for non-registered users to view different types of statistics related to reports. One focuses on categorical breakdowns, and the other on temporal trends, but both contribute to the overarching goal of making reporting data publicly accessible for informational purposes.

branch_008.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps for office staff to perform an initial review of reports. This includes identifying reports awaiting review, accessing their full details, and documenting internal observations during the review process.

branch_009.rationale: These operations collectively describe the process by which office staff evaluate citizen reports and make a formal decision regarding their acceptance or rejection, including providing necessary justifications for rejections. They all contribute to the initial handling and disposition of incoming reports.

branch_010.rationale: These low-level goals collectively define the various states a report can assume throughout its lifecycle, from initial submission to different stages of processing and eventual outcomes. They describe how the report's status is set and updated, either automatically by the system or manually by office staff, to reflect its current position in the workflow.

branch_011.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the process of identifying approved reports that require assignment, performing the actual assignment to either internal departments or external personnel/companies, and receiving system support for making informed assignment decisions. They all contribute to the overarching objective of ensuring that approved reports are efficiently and correctly directed to the appropriate entities for further action.

branch_012.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Monitor Report Progress
branch_012.rationale: These operations collectively provide the technical office staff with comprehensive capabilities to view, track, and report on the current status, historical changes, and overall progress of reports and issues assigned to their office. They all contribute to effective oversight and information retrieval regarding report lifecycle management.

branch_013.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps for technical office staff to track the progress and document the outcome of work performed on a report, from the initiation of active work to its successful completion and the detailed recording of how it was resolved. They all contribute to effectively managing the lifecycle of a report's resolution.

branch_014.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage communication with external maintenance personnel regarding assigned reports
branch_014.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete lifecycle of communication between technical office staff and external maintenance personnel concerning a specific report: sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire interaction history. These operations are all integral to effectively managing and tracking communication related to assigned reports.

branch_015.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Assigned Reports for External Maintenance Personnel
branch_015.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps an external maintenance personnel takes to identify, understand, and formally accept responsibility for reports assigned to them. These operations are all part of the initial phase of managing an assigned report, from discovery to formal acknowledgment.

branch_016.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate External Maintenance Personnel Reporting of Work Progress and Completion
branch_016.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the essential actions for external maintenance personnel to report the lifecycle of their assigned tasks. They cover initiating work, marking it as finished, and providing necessary evidence, all contributing to a comprehensive reporting process for maintenance activities.

branch_017.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable External Maintenance Personnel to Communicate with the Municipal Technical Office regarding Reports
branch_017.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the essential functionalities for external maintenance personnel to engage in two-way communication (sending and receiving messages) and maintain an auditable record (viewing history) with the municipal technical office concerning specific reports. They all contribute to establishing and managing this communication channel.

branch_018.rationale: All low-level goals describe various administrative tasks performed by a municipal administrator to set up, customize, and maintain the operational parameters, user access, data structures, and external interfaces of the system. They collectively aim to ensure the system functions according to municipal policies and integrates effectively.

branch_019.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Municipal Administrator to Monitor and Analyze System Performance and Usage
branch_019.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe various methods for the municipal administrator to access, customize, visualize, and export statistical data and reports. These operations are all geared towards providing the administrator with the necessary tools to monitor system performance, understand user interactions, evaluate system health, and conduct in-depth analysis of operational data.

branch_001.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is supported by the documentation and represents a distinct, independently satisfiable stakeholder outcome for the Citizen actor. While the bottom-up reconstruction suggests including 'Register', registration is a prerequisite for the account lifecycle rather than the core functional outcome of reporting. The sibling goal 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a specific attribute/option within the submission process, not a separate end-to-end outcome that would make 'Submit' redundant. The goal is correctly scoped to the act of reporting issues, which is the primary value proposition for the citizen in this context. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect because llg_003 ('UploadCitizenProfilePhoto') is unsupported by the documentation in the context of the parent goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports'. While the documentation mentions that users can upload a personal photo in the 'user settings panel' (Section C), this is a profile management feature, not a prerequisite or component of the act of submitting an urban issue report. Including it under this HLG conflates account profile customization with the core reporting workflow. Additionally, the parent goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' implies the complete process of creating a report, which includes the mandatory selection of the anonymity option (Section A: 'the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'). Although there is a sibling HLG 'Maintain Report Anonymity', the act of *selecting* this option is part of the submission form flow. However, the most critical error is the inclusion of the profile photo upload, which is unrelated to the submission act. The registration steps (llg_001, llg_002) are prerequisites, which is acceptable in a bottom-up decomposition if the HLG is interpreted as 'Enable Citizen to Submit', but strictly speaking, 'Submit' is the action. Given the strict instruction to audit every LLG for support in the parent context, llg_003 is clearly out of scope for 'Submit Urban Issue Reports'.

high_level_evaluation.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. While the bottom-up reconstruction suggests including 'Register', registration is a prerequisite for the account lifecycle rather than the core functional outcome of reporting. The sibling goal 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a specific attribute/option within the submission process, not a separate end-to-end outcome that would make 'Submit' redundant. The goal is correctly scoped to the act of reporting issues, which is the primary value proposition for the citizen in this context.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_010.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REMOVE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. They do not manage the entire lifecycle states such as 'Work in Progress', 'Suspended', or final resolution, which are handled by the Technical Office or External Maintenance Personnel. Furthermore, the actor already has two specific HLGs: 'Review Citizen Reports' and 'Approve or Reject Reports'. 'Manage Report Workflow' is a redundant umbrella term that overlaps with these specific goals and incorrectly implies responsibility for the entire lifecycle. Since the specific actions (review and approve/reject) are already covered by sibling HLGs, and the generic 'workflow management' is not a distinct stakeholder outcome for this actor (it is a system mechanism), this goal should be removed to avoid fragmentation and inaccuracy.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

Rewrite the functional intention for actor 'Municipal Administrator' using this focus: Express the broader intention of managing system configuration, user access, and administrative settings to ensure the system operates according to municipal policies.

actor.name: Municipal Administrator
actor.description: A municipal employee responsible for system configuration, user management, and accessing private statistics.

branch_019.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' is supported by the documentation, which states that the private section is accessible only to administrators and allows viewing public statistics plus charts and tables. The actor description explicitly lists 'accessing private statistics' as a responsibility. The goal is distinct from 'Configure System Settings' and represents an independent stakeholder outcome (monitoring/analysis) rather than a workflow phase of another goal. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Municipal Administrator to Monitor and Analyze System Performance and Usage' is semantically equivalent but slightly more verbose; the original goal is precise, supported, and appropriately scoped at the High-Level granularity. It does not suffer from fragmentation or redundancy relative to other Municipal Administrator goals. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain multiple capabilities that are not supported by the project description. Specifically, 'GenerateCustomStatisticalReports' (llg_002) implies a feature for defining custom parameters, which is not mentioned in the documentation (only predefined public stats and private charts/tables are described). 'ExportStatisticsData' (llg_003) is entirely unsupported as there is no mention of data export functionality. 'ViewPerformanceDashboards' (llg_004) introduces 'system health metrics' and 'KPIs' which are not part of the documented statistics (which focus on report counts, categories, and trends). Only 'RetrieveAllReportStatistics' (llg_001) is partially supported, but even its description of 'user interactions' is not explicitly detailed in the statistics section. The essential capability of viewing private charts and tables is not explicitly captured as a distinct LLG, and the existing LLGs introduce significant unsupported functionality.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for NO_MISSING_HIGH_LEVEL_GOALS. The project description outlines functional requirements for citizens (reporting, updates, communication, anonymity, monitoring), non-registered users (public view, public stats), organization office staff (review, approve/reject, workflow), technical office staff (assignment, tracking, status updates, internal communication), external maintenance personnel (task receipt, status updates, communication), and municipal administrators (configuration, private statistics). All these responsibilities are explicitly covered by the current High-Level Goals. Specifically, the 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' HLG for the Municipal Administrator covers the requirement to view private statistics (charts and tables) in addition to public ones. No other actor-level functional responsibilities are left uncovered.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Register and Report Urban Issues
branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (llg_001, llg_002, llg_003) focus on establishing and personalizing a citizen's account, which is a prerequisite for participating in the system. The subsequent goals (llg_004, llg_005, llg_006, llg_007) detail the process of submitting comprehensive reports about urban issues. Together, these operations form a complete flow for citizens to engage with a platform designed for reporting community problems.

branch_002.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Their Submitted Reports
branch_002.rationale: The low-level goals collectively aim to provide citizens with comprehensive tools to track the status and history of their submitted reports, receive timely updates, and control their notification preferences. This ensures citizens are well-informed and have agency over their interactions with the reporting system.

branch_003.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire conversation history. This ensures effective and transparent interaction for report resolution.

branch_004.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of allowing citizens to submit reports without their identity being publicly disclosed. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose this option, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it, ensuring the anonymity is maintained.

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Access and Monitor Public Reports
branch_005.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe functionalities that allow citizens to discover (view, filter) and track (subscribe, unsubscribe) publicly available reports submitted by other citizens. These operations are all geared towards providing citizens with the means to stay informed about and engage with community-reported information.

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to Access and View Public Reports
branch_006.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions by a non-registered user to retrieve, display, and filter public reports using various interfaces and methods. They collectively contribute to the overarching goal of making public reports accessible and viewable to non-registered users.

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable non-registered users to view various report statistics
branch_007.rationale: Both low-level goals describe functionalities for non-registered users to access and view different types of statistics related to reports: one by category and another showing trends over time. They collectively contribute to the broader goal of providing comprehensive statistical insights to non-registered users.

branch_008.rationale: These operations collectively describe the process by which office staff evaluate citizen reports and make a formal decision regarding their acceptance or rejection, including providing necessary justifications for rejections. They all contribute to the initial handling and disposition of incoming reports.

branch_009.rationale: These low-level goals collectively define the various states a report can assume throughout its lifecycle, from initial submission to different stages of processing and eventual outcomes. They describe how the report's status is set and updated, either automatically by the system or manually by office staff, to reflect its current position in the workflow.

branch_010.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the process of identifying approved reports that require assignment, performing the actual assignment to either internal departments or external personnel/companies, and receiving system support for making informed assignment decisions. They all contribute to the overarching objective of ensuring that approved reports are efficiently and correctly directed to the appropriate entities for further action.

branch_011.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Monitor and Report on Report Progress
branch_011.rationale: The low-level goals collectively aim to provide technical office staff with comprehensive capabilities to view current status, track historical changes, and generate summary reports related to the progress of reports or issues. These operations are all essential for effective oversight, management, and communication regarding the lifecycle and resolution of reports within their office.

branch_012.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the actions required by technical office staff to track the progress of a report from the initiation of active work to its successful completion, including documenting the specific details of how it was resolved. These operations are integral to overseeing and completing the resolution of a report.

branch_013.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage communication with external maintenance personnel regarding assigned reports
branch_013.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete lifecycle of communication between technical office staff and external maintenance personnel concerning a specific report: sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire interaction history. These operations are all integral to effectively managing and tracking communication related to assigned reports.

branch_014.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Assigned Reports for External Maintenance Personnel
branch_014.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps an external maintenance personnel takes to identify, understand, and formally accept responsibility for reports assigned to them. These operations are all part of the initial phase of managing an assigned report, from discovery to formal acknowledgment.

branch_015.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Update Maintenance Report Progress and Completion

branch_001.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is supported by the documentation, which details the process of selecting a map point, filling out a form, attaching photos, and choosing anonymity. However, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Citizens to Register and Report Urban Issues' suggests that registration is part of this goal. The documentation states that registration is a prerequisite ('Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered'), but it is a distinct lifecycle event with its own confirmation flow (email link). In Goal-Oriented Requirements Engineering, 'Register' is typically a separate High-Level Goal because it establishes the user's identity and access rights, whereas 'Submit Reports' is the primary functional interaction. The current hierarchy does not have a specific 'Register' HLG for the Citizen, but 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is the core functional outcome described in Section A. The reconstruction conflates the prerequisite (registration) with the main activity (reporting). The original goal is appropriately scoped to the act of reporting. While registration is necessary, it is not the same intention as reporting an issue. Therefore, the original goal is precise and supported. The lack of a separate 'Register' HLG is a potential gap, but it does not invalidate the 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' goal. The goal is not redundant with other Citizen goals (Receive Updates, Communicate, Maintain Anonymity, Monitor Community Issues). 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a specific option within the submission process, but it is often treated as a distinct quality/functional requirement in such systems. However, 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is the primary outcome. The reconstruction is less precise because it bundles registration. The original is better. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect. LLG llg_003 ('UploadCitizenProfilePhoto') is unsupported by the documentation in the context of the 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' goal. The documentation mentions uploading a personal photo only in the context of the 'user settings panel' (Section C), which is distinct from the report submission workflow (Section A). Including it here conflates profile management with report submission. Additionally, the parent goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is primarily about the act of reporting. While registration is a prerequisite, the core functional capability of 'Selecting Anonymity' (explicitly stated in Section A as part of the submission process: 'the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous') is missing from the LLGs. Although there is a sibling HLG 'Maintain Report Anonymity', the specific action of selecting this option during submission is a direct part of the 'Submit' workflow described in Section A. However, the most critical error is the inclusion of the unsupported profile photo upload in this specific goal context. The registration steps (llg_001, llg_002) are prerequisites, but often treated as separate goals; however, given the reconstructed HLG 'Enable Citizens to Register and Report Urban Issues', they are acceptable. The primary issue is llg_003 being out of scope for 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' and the missing explicit step for choosing anonymity which is part of the submission form interaction.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

The original High-Level Goal 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' is supported by the documentation, which states that in the private section accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view public statistics, charts, and tables. However, the goal is framed as a CRUD-like capability ('Access') rather than the stakeholder intention. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Monitor and Analyze System Performance and Usage' better captures the intent behind viewing these statistics (oversight and analysis). While 'Access' is not strictly wrong, 'Monitor and Analyze' is more precise regarding the *why* of the goal. Given the rubric's preference for intentional granularity over mere capability, and the fact that the original description already mentions 'for system oversight and analysis', the original goal is acceptable but slightly less precise than the reconstruction. missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for NO_MISSING_HIGH_LEVEL_GOALS. The retired goal 'Review Citizen Reports' is fully covered by the current HLGs 'Process Citizen Reports' and 'Approve or Reject Reports' for the Organization Office Staff. The project description explicitly states that the Organization Office performs a 'preliminary review' to mark reports as 'accepted or rejected'. The current HLG 'Approve or Reject Reports' directly captures this decision-making outcome, while 'Process Citizen Reports' covers the broader workflow of handling incoming reports. No other actor-level responsibilities from the description (Citizen, Non-Registered User, Technical Office Staff, External Maintenance Personnel, Municipal Administrator) are left uncovered by the current HLG list. All explicit functional requirements regarding submission, updates, communication, anonymity, monitoring, public access, statistics, workflow management, assignment, tracking, status updates, internal communication, task reception, work status updates, external communication, configuration, and comprehensive statistics are entailed by the existing goals.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Register and Report Urban Issues
branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (llg_001, llg_002, llg_003) focus on establishing and personalizing a citizen's account, which is a prerequisite for participating in the system. The subsequent goals (llg_004, llg_005, llg_006, llg_007) detail the process of submitting comprehensive reports about urban issues. Together, these operations form a complete flow for citizens to engage with a platform designed for reporting community problems.

branch_002.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire conversation history. This ensures effective and transparent interaction for report resolution.

branch_003.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable citizens to submit anonymous reports
branch_003.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of providing and maintaining anonymity for citizens when they submit reports. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose anonymity, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it.

branch_004.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Citizen monitors public reports submitted by other citizens.
branch_004.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe how a citizen can discover, organize, and stay informed about public reports submitted by other citizens, which are all facets of monitoring these reports.

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to Access and View Public Reports
branch_005.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions by a non-registered user to retrieve, display, and filter public reports using various interfaces and methods. They collectively contribute to the overarching goal of making public reports accessible and viewable to non-registered users.

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Access to Reporting Statistics
branch_006.rationale: Both low-level goals describe functionalities for non-registered users to view different types of statistics related to reports. One focuses on categorical breakdowns, and the other on temporal trends, but both contribute to the overarching goal of making reporting data publicly accessible for informational purposes.

branch_007.rationale: These operations collectively describe the process by which office staff evaluate citizen reports and make a formal decision regarding their acceptance or rejection, including providing necessary justifications for rejections. They all contribute to the initial handling and disposition of incoming reports.

branch_008.rationale: These low-level goals collectively define the various states a report can assume throughout its lifecycle, from initial submission to different stages of processing and eventual outcomes. They describe how the report's status is set and updated, either automatically by the system or manually by office staff, to reflect its current position in the workflow.

branch_009.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the process of identifying approved reports that require assignment, performing the actual assignment to either internal departments or external personnel/companies, and receiving system support for making informed assignment decisions. They all contribute to the overarching objective of ensuring that approved reports are efficiently and correctly directed to the appropriate entities for further action.

branch_010.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Monitor Report Progress
branch_010.rationale: These operations collectively provide the technical office staff with comprehensive capabilities to view, track, and report on the current status, historical changes, and overall progress of reports and issues assigned to their office. They all contribute to effective oversight and information retrieval regarding report lifecycle management.

branch_011.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the actions required by technical office staff to track the progress of a report from the initiation of active work to its successful completion, including documenting the specific details of how it was resolved. These operations are integral to overseeing and completing the resolution of a report.

branch_012.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Communication with External Maintenance Personnel
branch_012.rationale: These operations collectively describe the full lifecycle of communication between technical office staff and external maintenance personnel regarding assigned reports, including sending messages, receiving replies, and reviewing the complete interaction history. branch_001.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original HLG 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is supported by the documentation and represents a distinct stakeholder outcome (reporting a problem) separate from monitoring, communicating, or maintaining anonymity. While the bottom-up reconstruction suggests including 'Register', registration is a prerequisite for the actor to exist in the system and is typically handled as a separate onboarding goal or implicit precondition rather than being merged into the core functional goal of reporting. The current HLG correctly isolates the act of submitting reports. The sibling HLGs cover the other distinct citizen intentions (monitoring, communicating, anonymity, community monitoring). Therefore, the original goal is appropriately scoped and should be kept. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect. LLG llg_003 ('UploadCitizenProfilePhoto') is unsupported by the documentation in the context of the 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' goal. The documentation states that citizens can upload a personal photo in the 'user settings panel' (Section C), which is a profile management feature, not a prerequisite or component of the report submission workflow. Including it under 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is a misattribution of responsibility. Additionally, the parent goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' implies the core action of creating a report, which is covered by llg_004, llg_005, llg_006, and llg_007. However, the inclusion of registration steps (llg_001, llg_002) is acceptable as prerequisites for the actor to perform the goal, but the profile photo upload is not part of the submission flow. Therefore, the decomposition must be corrected to remove the unsupported profile photo capability from this specific HLG.

branch_002.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for REMOVE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original HLG 'Communicate with Administration' is supported by the documentation (Section C: 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply'). However, it is semantically redundant with the sibling HLG 'Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Their Submitted Reports'. The description of the sibling HLG explicitly includes 'receive timely updates' and 'fostering transparency and trust', which encompasses the communication aspect. In goal-oriented requirements engineering, the ability to receive status updates and exchange messages regarding a specific report is typically part of the broader intention to monitor and manage that report's lifecycle. Keeping a separate HLG for communication fragments the citizen's interaction with the report lifecycle. The sibling HLG is a better umbrella for all post-submission interactions (monitoring status, receiving notifications, and communicating). Therefore, the specific communication goal should be removed to consolidate the hierarchy under the broader management/monitoring goal.

branch_003.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REMOVE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original HLG 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is supported by the documentation (Section A: 'system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'). However, it is semantically redundant with the sibling HLG 'Submit Urban Issue Reports'. The act of submitting a report inherently includes the choice of anonymity as a configuration option during the submission workflow. In goal-oriented requirements engineering, a specific attribute or option within a primary workflow (submission) is typically not an independent High-Level Goal unless it represents a distinct, independently satisfiable stakeholder outcome separate from the main action. Here, the citizen's intention is to 'submit a report', and anonymity is a property of that submission. Keeping it as a separate HLG fragments the submission workflow. The sibling 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is the appropriate umbrella for the entire submission process, including the anonymity choice. Therefore, the specific anonymity goal should be removed to consolidate the hierarchy under the broader submission goal.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.
